title: NIH Vaccine Research Center → Moderna mRNA-1273 (Spikevax)
summary: NIAID Vaccine Research Center (VRC) scientists and academic collaborators published a method in 2017 for holding coronavirus spike proteins in their prefusion shape. In January 2020 the VRC and Moderna, a Flagship Pioneering company incorporated in 2009, finalized the sequence of the mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine, which NIH says was developed by NIAID scientists and Moderna; NIH ran the first human trial and Moderna commercialized it as Spikevax. In December 2022 Moderna licensed NIAID's spike-stabilization patents non-exclusively and paid a $400 million catch-up royalty. A separate 2021 dispute over naming NIH scientists as co-inventors on Moderna's mRNA-sequence patent application had no resolution in the sources reviewed. NIH research continued: this is co-development, not a hand-over.

links.claim: Moderna's 10-K states that in December 2022 it entered a non-exclusive patent license with NIAID covering patent rights on stabilizing prefusion coronavirus spike proteins for COVID-19 vaccines, agreed to low single-digit royalties on future net sales plus minimum annual royalties and milestones, and made a $400 million catch-up royalty payment to NIAID that month.

claims.claim: The government (NIH) invented the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine.
claims.explanation: NIH describes mRNA-1273 as developed by NIAID scientists together with Moderna, and Moderna licensed NIAID's spike-stabilization patents. But the mRNA platform is Moderna's, and inventorship of the vaccine's mRNA sequence was disputed: Moderna said its scientists invented the sequence, while NIH maintained its scientists should be co-inventors for work on the protein sequence.

claims.claim: Moderna's $400 million payment settled its inventorship dispute with NIH.
claims.explanation: Moderna's 10-K describes the $400 million as a catch-up royalty under a license to NIAID's prefusion spike-stabilization patents. The inventorship dispute concerned a different application, on the vaccine's mRNA sequence, which Moderna said in December 2021 it would not pursue for now while talks continued. No source reviewed shows the payment resolving that dispute.

sources.title: Moderna, Inc. Form 10-K for fiscal year 2022

claims.claim: The $400 million payment was small relative to Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine revenue.
claims.explanation: Moderna's 10-K reports COVID-19 vaccine product sales of $17.7 billion in 2021 and $18.4 billion in 2022 (about $36.1 billion), so the $400 million catch-up royalty was roughly 1.1% of those two years' sales. Public Citizen, an advocacy group, made the same comparison. Ongoing royalties are described only as low single digits.
